endorsements.quote: At the institutional level, a designated AI governance committee or equivalent multidisciplinary body should approve AI deployment within specific workflows, define local validation requirements, and oversee monitoring and escalation pathways.

At the institutional level, a designated AI governance committee or equivalent multidisciplinary body should approve AI deployment within specific workflows, define local validation requirements, and oversee monitoring and escalation pathways.

Physicians retain responsibility for interpreting outputs; accepting, modifying, or rejecting recommendations; completing required disclosure and consent processes; and signing off on clinically consequential decisions [ 24 31 ].

Accountability should be distributed in proportion to operational control: physicians remain responsible for case-specific clinical judgment; institutions remain responsible for local validation, workflow integration, and performance monitoring; and developers remain responsible for model design, governance update, and management of known limitations [ 22 32 ].

To operationalize safe delegation, institutions should apply automation scope of practice (ASoP) through a stepwise decision process that links task classification, verification triggers, and authority allocation [ 23 24 32 ].
Routine safety governance includes monitoring of override rates, bypass patterns, and clinician-reported burden to ensure that safeguards remain salient rather than becoming background noise [ 25 ].
Organizational policy should align incentives with safety rather than throughput alone [ 23 37 38 ].

Institutions should ensure that physician training shifts from basic AI literacy to verification-oriented competencies and calibrated trust, defined as the ability to adjust reliance on AI according to clinical context, risk level, and uncertainty signals [ 26 27 ].
Skill retention activities should be risk stratified and targeted to high-risk or high-delegation workflows.
Institutions should maintain a local learning-oriented, nonpunitive error taxonomy.

For institutions considering adoption, implementation should proceed incrementally, beginning with governance structures and bounded pilot workflows followed by prospective monitoring, recalibration, and staged expansion, with skill retention monitoring and incentive alignment incorporated from the outset rather than after scale-up [ 13 43 44 ].
Physicians should also appraise the provenance and recency of model-cited evidence to determine whether AI-synthesized rationales should be accepted, discounted, or escalated [ 30 ].
Attestation interfaces are designed to discourage verbatim or formulaic rationales, with free-text fields structured to elicit clinical specificity rather than generic confirmation.

unlisted_practices: Classify verification triggers using a structured matrix based on clinical harm severity, irreversibility and time criticality, uncertainty or conflict intensity, and equity sensitivity.
Predefine equity-sensitive contexts using local validation results, known subgroup performance gaps, and high-impact domains.
Use demographic variables for bias surveillance rather than to justify differential clinical treatment.
Disclose AI involvement and relevant uncertainty to patients, tailored to risk level and use case, using standardized plain-language phrasing and risk-stratified consent workflows.
Convene focused interprofessional review with pharmacists, nurses, and specialists for prespecified high-risk scenarios while physicians retain final authority.
Establish protected safety investment funding time for complex case consultation, interprofessional review training, and skill retention activities.
Reserve mandatory pauses and other high-interruption mechanisms for high-risk decisions, using passive cues for lower-risk situations.
Record AI-output conflicts with guidelines or physician judgment, with review, attestation, and rationale, in the audit log.
Classify AI tasks into tiered automation scope of practice, moving tasks to more restrictive tiers dynamically when risk conditions arise.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint article proposing a multilevel governance framework for physician resilience, shared authority, verification, and skill preservation when integrating generative AI into clinical workflows.
